q: A peppery Friulian red also known as Ribolla Nera was rescued from near extinction in the 1970s. Name the grape.
exp: It was left off the permitted list after the war and survived in a few old plots around Prepotto until growers pushed to have it reinstated. The black pepper note comes from rotundone, the same compound that marks cool-climate Syrah.

q: Iron-red soil over fissured limestone on the Slovenian border grows Vitovska and Terrano. Name that plateau.
exp: The karst is riddled with sinkholes and caves, and the little soil there is collects in pockets between bare rock. The bora wind off the northeast is fierce enough to shape how vines are trained.

q: Skin-fermented Ribolla Gialla made one border village the address most associated with Friulian orange wine. Name the village.
exp: Long skin macerations were revived there in the mid-1990s, in wood, and buried Georgian qvevri followed with Gravner's 2001 vintage. Ribolla Gialla suits the treatment because its skins are thick and its acidity high.

q: Deep-coloured Lagrein has its historic home in one quarter on the edge of Bolzano. Which one?
exp: The alluvial gravel at Gries is warm and free-draining, which suits a late-ripening variety on a valley floor. Lagrein is a descendant of Teroldego and shows the same dark colour and bitter-cherry edge.

q: Italy's first denomination created specifically for traditional-method sparkling wine sits in the mountains along the upper Adige. Which denomination?
exp: Trento was recognised in 1993 for metodo classico alone, drawing on vineyards planted high on both valley walls. Altitude supplies the acidity that a base wine for sparkling needs.

q: Pinot Bianco that stays fresh for decades comes from a village on porphyry sand west of Bolzano. Name that village.
exp: The sandy quartz porphyry soils are unusually rich in potassium, which growers there credit for the wine's structure and longevity. Old bottles are released from the cellar as Rarita after at least ten years on the lees.

q: Sylvaner, Kerner and Gruner Veltliner grow up a narrow valley running from Bolzano toward the Brenner pass. Name that valley.
exp: It is the coldest and highest of Alto Adige's zones, which is why the grape list reads more Austrian than Italian. The wines are lean, high-acid and aromatic rather than broad.

q: Trentino's one notable native white is dried on racks until Holy Week to make the region's Vino Santo. Name the grape.
exp: The drying runs about six months, far longer than most passito, and botrytis is welcomed on the way. The name comes from nocciola, hazelnut, which is what the dry version tastes of.

q: Mozart's Don Giovanni calls for a dark, soft red from Trentino by name in its final act. Name the grape.
exp: Isera in the Vallagarina is its stronghold, on basalt soils south of Rovereto. The wine is fragrant and low in tannin, meant to be drunk within a few years rather than kept.

q: Pigato turned out under DNA analysis to be the same variety as a white already planted the length of the northwest coast. Which one?
exp: Pigato is a mutation of Vermentino with freckled skins, which is what the name records. Growers still bottle the two separately because the clones behave differently in the vineyard and in the glass.

q: One Lambrusco sets fruit so poorly that its wine comes out pale pink and unusually sharp. Which one?
exp: Sorbara flowers badly and drops much of its crop, leaving thin bunches with little colour to give. Grasparossa at the other end of the scale is dark, tannic and much fuller bodied.

q: The first Italian white ever raised to DOCG, back in 1987, grows in the hills of Romagna. Name the grape.
exp: The promotion was controversial at the time because the wine was thought not to merit it, and it pushed the authorities to be stricter afterwards. Albana has thick skins, so it takes to both skin contact and drying for passito.

q: Grapes dried in lofts above the terraced cliffs of the Cinque Terre make a rare sweet wine sold in small bottles. Name it.
exp: Bosco leads the blend with Albarola and Vermentino alongside, all of it carried off terraces reachable only on foot or by rack railway. Yields after drying are so small that a few bottles come from a whole day's picking.

q: Green walnut, curry spice and a saline edge: whichever village makes it, vin jaune begins as a single permitted variety. Name it.
exp: Savagnin is the whole recipe: not even Chardonnay, the Jura's most planted grape, may enter a vin jaune. A member of the Traminer family, it hangs late into the autumn and keeps the acidity that carries the wine through its long years in cask.

q: From harvest to the earliest legal bottling, the wine that will become vin jaune waits longer in cask than any other unfortified wine of France. State the minimum wait.
accept: six years and three months in cask
six years and three months in barrel
six years and three months in oak
six years and three months from harvest
at least six years and three months
minimum of six years and three months
six years and three months minimum
minimum six years and three months
six years and three months under the veil
six years and three months under voile
six years and three months of ageing
six years and three months of aging
six years and three months ageing
six years and three months aging
exp: Six years and three months separate the picking from the bottle, and for at least sixty of those months the voile of yeast must be at work on the untopped cask. Nothing is refilled as the level falls, and over a third of the wine is surrendered to the air before a drop is sold.

q: Just 62 centilitres, squat and heavy-shouldered: the law reserves one bottle for the Jura's vin jaune and permits it no other. Name it.
exp: The clavelin holds what is left of a litre, so the story runs, after the years of evaporation under the voile, the missing thirty-eight centilitres having gone to the angels. French law reserves the shape for vin jaune, so the bottle announces the style across the room.
